Pele Yoetz 339:2: And it is fitting for a person to strive to do everyone's will and not to cause grief to anyone for his own benefit and the like, provided there is no nullification of the Creator's will, for they said in the Talmud (Shabbat 118b): Rabbi Yose said, “In all my days I never transgressed the words of my colleagues; I know of myself that I am not a Kohen, yet if my colleagues told me to go up to the platform [to bless the people like the Kohanim], I would go up.” Learn from this how much one must set aside his own understanding and nullify his own will for the sake of his fellow's will. And they further said in the Talmud (Gittin 68b) that Ashmedai, king of the demons, was once walking with Benayahu ben Yehoyada, and he saw a blind man losing his way on the road; he gave him his hand and led him back onto the road. He said, “This one is a perfectly righteous man, and it is proclaimed about him in heaven that whoever does him a favor merits the World to Come.” He then saw a drunk man losing his way on the road; he gave him his hand and led him back onto the road. He said, “This one is a perfectly wicked man, and it is proclaimed about him in heaven that whoever does him a favor, so that he may consume his [reward for his] world in this life, merits the World to Come” — thus far. And from this too a person should learn how good it is to do everyone's will, wherever there is no nullification of the Creator's will — for then he should nullify the will of the entire world and his own will, and not nullify the will of the blessed Creator. And this too requires a scale and balances of justice, for great is human dignity, and sometimes one must be sociable with people and not give the many occasion to sin and speak wrongly of him — these are matters without fixed measure, and every shrewd man should act with knowledge and choose the straight path for himself.
Pele Yoetz 339:3: And it is known that a person's own will is his honor, and those who press a man to honor him with something he does not want — such as making him eat at their table or seating him among the great, and the like, thereby overriding his will and causing him grief — do not do well; this is not honor but disgrace. Go and learn from Rabbi Yishmael, whose mother wanted to wash his feet and drink his bathwater, and he did not want to accept it, until the sages told him that her will was her honor (Yerushalmi Peah 1:1). And it all depends on what kind of person he appears to be: if it seems that he wants the thing and that his will is that they press him until he is embarrassed, do his will as his will, and this is a sign and wonder that he desires kindness, and it shall be counted as a commandment for him, and let his reward be repaid according to his deed, and may his will be done, peace be within his ranks.
Pele Yoetz 340:1: Ro'eh (Shepherd) — It is written (Isaiah 40:11), “Like a shepherd He shall tend His flock, with His arm He shall gather the lambs, and carry them in His bosom, gently leading those with young.” And it is known that every leader of Israel is called a shepherd, as it is written (Numbers 27:17), “And the congregation of the Lord shall not be like sheep that have no shepherd.” And from this verse one can learn how the leader of the community must shepherd Israel: for just as the shepherd gathers the lambs with his arm so that they not scatter here and there and be lost, so the shepherd of Israel must exert great effort to see that there be unity among them and that quarrels and disputes not arise among them, for they said (Tanchuma, Tzav 7; Shoftim 18) that even if they worship idolatry, since they are in unity (in one group), the attribute of judgment has no power over them, as it is written (Hosea 4:17), “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone.” But if their heart is divided, now they shall bear guilt.
Pele Yoetz 340:2: And just as the shepherd carries in his bosom the sick and the young who cannot walk, so the shepherd of Israel must bear with those of lesser stature, lacking in knowledge, and carry them according to their measure, as a nursemaid carries the suckling infant. And just as the shepherd gently leads the nursing ewes according to their strength, so the shepherd of Israel should not burden the congregation nor make it too heavy for them, even to fulfill every good thing and to afflict the soul, but rather according to each one's strength, and according to what kind of person he is, and according to the place and the time, and according to what his eyes see — so shall he conduct himself, lest they cast off the yoke.
Pele Yoetz 340:3: And just as our teacher Moses, when he ran after the kid, and upon reaching the water it stopped to drink, said to it, “You were thirsty and I did not know it; now you are tired,” and carried it on his shoulder (Shemot Rabbah 2:2), so the shepherd of Israel, when a person opposes him and wearies him, should find merit for him and have compassion on him. Let the wise man hear such things and add learning, and let him conduct himself toward his people's flock and guard them like a shepherd tending his flock, for the honor of his Maker.
Pele Yoetz 341:1: The letter Shin: Shalom (Peace) — It is written (Psalms 34:15), “Seek peace and pursue it.” And we have likewise learned: be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace (Avot 1:12). And from the statements of our sages, of blessed memory, in the Talmud and Midrashim, and in the chapter on peace, and the books of ethics full of splendor, all testify and declare how great is peace and how hated is dispute. And the sages spoke only of one whom dispute pursues while he flees from it, and peace flees from him while he pursues it — such a one is called a lover of peace and pursuer of peace, and his deeds are praised in the gates.
Pele Yoetz 341:2: And behold, if you should say to a man given to strife and contention, “Do you not know, if you have not heard, how great is peace and how hated is dispute?” (Sifrei, Naso 42), he would say, “I know, but who can restrain himself to be at peace with people who anger me to my face constantly, and jealousy is as hard as the grave?” Even so, say to him: if it were an easy matter, the Holy One, blessed be He, would not have set such a great reward for it, and peace would not be so great; but according to the pain is the reward. And this is comparable to one who is told from Heaven: “If you make peace with so-and-so, you shall live a thousand years, but if you make dispute, you shall die immediately” — without doubt he would endure anything, and it would seem easy to him to make peace, against the great benefit of dying versus living a thousand years. How much more so must a person strengthen himself in order not to die an eternal death, and in order to merit good reward for the World to Come, for one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come is better than all the life of this world (Avot 4:17). And how much more so in order to give satisfaction to his Creator and not to anger his Maker. Such things let the living take to heart regarding every difficult matter, and then “every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight” (Isaiah 40:4). And if peace is great between a man and his fellow, how much more so is peace in the home great between a man and his wife, and dispute hated — and I have already written of this above under the entry Machloket — see there.
Pele Yoetz 341:3: And it is not enough for a man to make peace for himself with everyone and increase the honor of his household, but also, when there is a dispute between people, or between a man and his wife, he should exert all his effort to bring peace between a person and his fellow and between a man and his wife, for this gives great satisfaction to his Creator. The proof is that this is among the things whose fruits a person eats in this world while the principal remains for him in the World to Come. And know that the Holy One, blessed be He, changed [the truth] for the sake of peace (Yevamot 65b; Bereishit Rabbah 48:21), and permitted His Name, written in holiness, to be erased for the sake of bringing peace (Bamidbar Rabbah 11:15; Chullin ch. 1, [a source]). And this was the trait of Aaron the Priest, who increased peace in the world, and regarding this they commanded (Avot, ibid.): be among the disciples of Aaron. And it is fitting for a great man to forgo his own honor and go to a lesser man for the sake of making peace, so that his own honor not exceed the honor of Heaven's Name, and the essence of this commandment's glory is among the great, for their words and conversation can remove the heart of stone with pleasant speech, and their words bear fruit, whether out of shame or out of honor. And this is why they said (Berachot 64a): Torah scholars increase peace in the world.
Pele Yoetz 341:4: And our sages, of blessed memory, further warned us and said (Avot 4:15): be first to greet every person. And they said of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai that he would greet every person first, even a gentile in the marketplace (Berachot 17a).
Pele Yoetz 341:5: And they said (ibid. 6:1[?]) that whoever is greeted and does not respond, regarding him it is said (Isaiah 3:14), “The plunder of the poor is in your houses” — read it as “the language of affliction.” And it is true that they said in the holy Zohar that it is not good to give greeting or return a greeting to a wicked man, for it brings evil upon oneself; in any case, one can say to anyone, in the manner people say in every language, “Good day,” and through this he is saved from mentioning “peace,” which is the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, in filthy alleyways. And how great is the obligation upon the wealthy and upon Torah scholars to greet everyone first, and especially the wretched poor, so that they not be suspected, out of their own pride, of despising them as vile and loathsome, Heaven forbid. And how often it happens that a poor man greets a wealthy man with a bashful face and a weak voice, so soft his voice is not heard, and the wealthy man, preoccupied in his thoughts with his affairs, does not respond, or responds in a whisper, and they come to suspect him and speak wrongly of him.
Pele Yoetz 341:6: Behold, therefore, how good it is to greet everyone first with a pleasant countenance and clear speech, and to inquire after everyone's welfare, and especially to say to a poor and needy person, “How are you, what are you doing, is all well?” And it shall be counted as a great commandment, for it gladdens the heart of the wretched and gives him a sense of worth. And how great is the punishment for one who does not concern himself with giving satisfaction to his fellow creatures, and especially to the wretched poor, in a matter that costs nothing but a word of the lips — this is nothing but an evil heart clothed in pride. But it is indeed true that it is not the way of the young to greet their elders first, as it is written (Job 29:8), “The young men saw me and hid.” And likewise it is not the way of the great to greet the very young first, since they must conduct themselves with a certain degree of dignity so that their reverence be imposed upon others; and furthermore, whatever is not proper conduct, one who changes it from the established way is at a disadvantage, and the matter is disgraceful in the eyes of all who see it. But to everyone else, let him greet first, and the Name shall call him “peace.”
Pele Yoetz 341:7: And when giving a greeting, one's mouth and heart must be equal, and he must not be among those of whom it is said (Jeremiah 9:7), “With his mouth he speaks peace to his fellow, but in his heart he sets an ambush for him,” for this is deceiving people's minds. And the Torah recorded regarding the tribes of Yah that from their disgrace we learn their praise, for since they hated Joseph, they could not speak peaceably to him. Therefore, if it seems to him that it is fitting and permitted for him to hate someone (in the manner written above under the entry Sinah), he should not seek his peace and welfare unless he asks out of fear. And regarding the matter of bringing peace between a man and his fellow, one must weigh with a scale whether they are among those for whom scattering is beneficial, etc., or among those for whom gathering is beneficial, etc.
Pele Yoetz 342:1: Sin'ah (Hatred) — Hatred is hateful, regarding which the Tanna said (Avot 2:11): hatred of creatures removes a person from the world. And it drags along many transgressions, for hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 6:14) and leads to dispute and to slander, and causes him to rejoice at calamity, to be one who injures and cheats, and to take revenge and bear a grudge like a snake, and many other such evils. And it is written in the books that among all transgressions, there is none that a person transgresses as constantly as hatred, for every single moment he transgresses what is written in the Torah (Leviticus 19:17), “You shall not hate your brother in your heart,” and what is written (ibid.), “And you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” And this is the reason the Holy Temple was destroyed because of the sin of baseless hatred. And every kind of hatred is called baseless hatred, for all the arguments a person has for hating are vanity, deceptive fabrications, as we have explained above under the entry Ahavat Re'im — see there.
Pele Yoetz 342:2: And the evil of hatred grows great when it is in the heart while outwardly he shows himself like a friend, like a brother — this is a grievous, incurable evil, for when hatred is public, in the end they will find someone to make peace between them, but when it is in the heart, it is an eternal, hidden transgression, and a person cannot guard himself against his fellow, for he will deceive him with the smoothness of his tongue, whose speech is smoother than butter, while in his heart he sets an ambush and works to bring down his fellow into a pit — and this is why the Torah commanded (Leviticus, ibid.), “You shall not hate your brother in your heart.” And it is good for a man to choose the lesser evil, and if his fellow has treated him badly, or in a manner that permits hating him because of his evil deeds, in the way our sages, of blessed memory, explained the verse (Exodus 23:5), “If you see the donkey of one who hates you,” then let him show his hatred openly. But the evil of man, when hatred is great, is due to jealousy, thinking that his fellow has cut into his livelihood, and therefore he is ashamed and afraid to show that this is why he hates him, for it is a disgrace for him to let everyone know that he is one of little faith, and hatred stirs up strife until eventually he finds many pretexts for the hatred; but in truth, wind shall carry them all away, as stated above.
Pele Yoetz 342:3: And according to the greatness of the evil of hatred, which caused the destruction of our holy and glorious House, and as long as we are not purified of this sin it is impossible to be redeemed, as our sages, of blessed memory, said: the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “You caused Me to destroy My house and burn My Temple through baseless hatred; seek peace and you shall be redeemed,” as it is said (Psalms 122:6), “Ask for the peace of Jerusalem.” And this is what the commentators explained regarding “you were sold for nothing” (Isaiah 52:3) — meaning, through the sin of baseless hatred you were sold, and not with money, that is, you shall not be redeemed with money [alone] but must rectify this sin. And according to the greatness of the merit of the commandment “And you shall love your neighbor as yourself,” which is a great principle in the Torah, it is fitting for a person to strengthen himself with great might and effort, through constant pure thoughts, to remove hatred from his heart and to be one who removes matzah [leaven, i.e., sourness] and brings in love — and especially with his wife, even if she is a bad woman, every fault in her being what fell to her lot, whether for good or ill it shall follow — let him gather great strength to love her as his own body, for great is the evil of one who hates his wife, for he sets his eyes on another woman and his children become children of hatred, evil seed, and woe to him who blemishes his own offspring. And let the man tremble and shrink from every matter of transgression, and especially regarding hatred and love, and especially between a man and his wife, considering that these are ancient matters, and through the deed below the deed above is aroused — either building worlds or destroying them — and hatred and dispute arouse strife and prosecution and separation above, while through love, brotherhood, peace, and friendship, love between the beloved is aroused above, and peace is made in the high places, and it brings about the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, and this is the reason our redemption and the ransom of our souls depend on this.
Pele Yoetz 342:4: Behold, therefore, let a man gather strength through pure thoughts to remove hatred from his heart, and if he cannot, let him go to a sage and tell him his trouble, and he shall rectify him with good counsel and a spirit of understanding. O people of the Name, let us be strong and strengthen ourselves for the sake of our God, and let us become united in love and brotherhood, peace and friendship — perhaps God will be entreated and remember the rose [Israel], and restore our captivity as before; so may it be [His] will, speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 342:5: And let the living take to heart what Scripture commanded (Leviticus 19:17), “You shall not hate your brother in your heart,” and “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (ibid.). There was no need to command regarding one who does good to him and toward whom he has no grievance, for from where would it come that he should hate him — he certainly loves him. Scripture needed to command only regarding one who is his enemy and seeks his harm; regarding this the Torah commanded not to hate him but to love him as his own body. And though it is a hard thing to repay good for evil, and people say that one who eats something bitter cannot spit something sweet, since our Creator has commanded us thus, learn from this that it is a thing that can be fulfilled, for the Torah was not given to the ministering angels, and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not act tyrannically with His creatures (Avodah Zarah 3a); rather, great effort and much persistence are needed to think thoughts that from the Most High comes both the evil and the good, for a person's own benefit, and no person can harm or benefit his fellow, or touch even a hairsbreadth of what is prepared for his fellow, without a decree of the Almighty, and the Omnipresent has many agents to do what is good in His eyes for a person's benefit in this world or the World to Come. Such and such things let the living take to heart and believe this with complete faith, and let him always strengthen himself with pure thoughts to remove hatred and arouse love, and according to the pain is the reward. And there is another principle they said (Avot 1:6): judge every person favorably, as it is written (Proverbs 21:2), “Every way of a man is upright in his own eyes.” Upon whom shall we rely? Upon our Father in Heaven — He shall rectify us with good counsel from before Him, and grant us merit to do what is good and upright in the eyes of God and man, Amen, so may it be [His] will.
Pele Yoetz 343:1: Shabbat — The merits of keeping Shabbat properly are known to be very great, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 118b): whoever keeps Shabbat properly, even if he worships idolatry like the generation of Enosh, is forgiven. And they further said (ibid.) that had Israel kept two Sabbaths properly, they would have been redeemed. And they further said (Shemot Rabbah 25:12; Midrash Tehillim 95) that keeping Shabbat is equal to the entire Torah. And in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 3:1; see Yerushalmi Ta'anit 1:1) they said that Israel shall be redeemed only through the merit of Shabbat. And I wished to copy the holy words of Mahari, of blessed memory, in the book Kikar LaAden (p. 140), what he wrote about this, and these are his words, abbreviated and with some added elaboration: according to the words of our sages, of blessed memory, it is exceedingly necessary to keep Shabbat so that the redemption come speedily in our days, and there is no way to bring healing and remedy to our souls except through the observance of Shabbat — even though we shall repent, everything depends on the observance of Shabbat. And truly, there are innumerable troubles regarding the matter of Shabbat observance, for through our sins we have been in this state for several hundred years, and this is why we have not been saved.
Pele Yoetz 343:2: And behold, praise to the blessed God, the vast majority of Israel are holy, keeping Shabbat and calling it a delight; however, great is the pain over two things that have been our undoing: that there are those who are not careful about speaking weekday matters on Shabbat, though the Merciful One said (Isaiah 58:13), “And speak a word,” and adjacent to it (ibid. 14), “then you shall delight in the Lord” — for if you guard your speech, then you shall delight in the Name, and He shall soon cause the scion of David to sprout. And the masses of the people do not know, do not understand, and do not believe that speaking weekday matters on Shabbat is considered a desecration of Shabbat, yet the matter is evident from its own context, for it is written (Exodus 23:12), “And on the seventh day you shall rest, for six days,” etc., “and on the seventh day is Shabbat” — it turns out that our Maker commanded us to rest just as Shabbat itself “rests,” and it does not “rest” from anything but speech, as it is written (Psalms 33:6), “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made.”
Pele Yoetz 343:3: And behold, to say, “I shall do this thing tomorrow”, regarding anything forbidden to do on Shabbat, is entirely forbidden according to everyone; and even if he prefaces it by saying, as some ignorant people are accustomed to say, “I shall do this thing, not by way of Shabbat speech,” it does not help and does not save him from the prohibition, and it is mockery and folly, for how can he say it is not Shabbat speech when he speaks falsely by saying it on Shabbat? And likewise there is a custom among ignorant people, when handling money, to say, “I am touching silver and gold, not money,” and many other such empty customs of the people who walk in darkness and have not seen the light of Torah. And behold, even though there is one who permits speaking and telling of matters that have already occurred, many disagree, and even regarding a matter necessary for a person, the Tosafot wrote (Shabbat 113b, s.v. “shelo,” and there in the name of the Yerushalmi) that one should minimize it, and only under pressing circumstances did they permit asking about someone's welfare on Shabbat, and the holy one was very stringent regarding the matter of speech.
Pele Yoetz 343:4: And there is a further transgression: telling a gentile [to do forbidden work], which is a sin committed through speech, and even if the gentile does it for the sake of an Israelite without being told to, it is forbidden to benefit from it, and many stumble in this by drinking coffee at inns, which is entirely forbidden, and through our many sins it has come to be treated as permitted by some people. And two have become three transgressions of speech: the two we mentioned — speaking of weekday matters and telling a gentile [to do forbidden work] — and the third is not speaking words of Torah and spending the holy day in idle words and outings, for Sabbaths were given only for engagement in Torah. And it is known what the early ones explained regarding the verse (Psalms 75:3), “When I take the appointed time, I shall judge with uprightness” — that whoever wastes time and does not engage in Torah on Sabbaths and festivals shall be punished also for the weekdays, and he has no room for exemption by saying he was busy earning his livelihood, for the Sabbaths and festivals shall prove that there is no truth in his mouth.
Pele Yoetz 343:5: And one must engage on Shabbat in the Written Torah and the Oral Torah, which hint at the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, and on Shabbat there is the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence; and also, it is through the merit of Torah that we shall be redeemed, for this redemption is through the merit of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, who demanded the honor of the Torah. These are the three transgressions of Israel regarding the desecration of Shabbat through speech. And a fourth: that they do not inquire and study the laws of Shabbat from the mouths of books or authors, and they have stumbled and fallen into many prohibitions of Shabbat and desecrate Shabbat even unwittingly, such as regarding the prohibitions of shevut, the prohibition of muktzeh, the prohibition of trapping, the prohibition of selecting, and the prohibition of laundering, and likewise regarding the matter of heating food, and especially at joyous celebrations, where there is much cause for stumbling, and the leaders of communities must stand in the breach. And there are many such matters, of which one who does not come to inquire, even when he grows old, will not know that there is a prohibition involved. And it is already written in Sefer Chasidim (section 154) that just as they said (Megillah 32a) that one must inquire and study the laws of Passover [before the holiday], so an obligation rests upon one to inquire and search to know the laws of Shabbat and go over them at least once a year. And an obligation rests upon the preachers to expound to the people the statutes of the Name and His teachings, and to those who hear and fulfill it shall be pleasant, and upon them shall come the blessing of good. And the kabbalists wrote that it is not only from desecration of Shabbat that one must be careful on Shabbat, but from any hint of transgression and sin whatsoever, for even the common person, whose sin on a weekday blemishes only the world of Asiyah, on Shabbat, when all the worlds are included one within another, also blemishes Atzilut. And through our sins, the sin of speaking forbidden words, which is exceedingly severe, is more common specifically on Shabbat, for since people are free, they make corners and synagogues of the common people, and there they speak to one another every kind of forbidden speech — let one who guards his soul distance himself from them, and not go out of his house except to associate with those who fear the Name and esteem His Name, who are engaged in Torah. And one who keeps Shabbat and conducts himself in it with holiness of thought, speech, and deed has a great key to acquire holiness for the weekdays easily and to grow in them with holiness of thought, speech, and deed; and if he strives during the weekdays to conduct himself with holiness of thought, speech, and deed, it shall be easy for him and he shall find help corresponding to him to acquire an additional measure of the holiness of Shabbat for his soul, spirit, and higher soul — as is his deed on weekdays, so is his deed on Shabbat, and as is his deed on Shabbat, so is his deed on weekdays. Therefore let a man gather strength to cling to his Maker on the holy Shabbat day with fear, love, and abundant joy and intense cleaving, and to engage in Torah according to his ability, and to guard against and distance himself utterly from every evil thing, and through this he shall find the means of his redemption. And let the living take to heart that one who desecrates Shabbat through speech or deed, besides that his sin is exceedingly great, also lengthens the exile and prevents the redemption of Israel and the building of the Holy Temple, and bears this humble one's [the author's] burden upon himself — for all this shall God bring into judgment. Indeed, Israel is holy but does not know the severity of the prohibition, and when the people hear, each shall help his fellow and say to his brother, “Be strong” — perhaps we shall merit to keep the Sabbaths of the Name properly, full of Torah and commandments, and the redeemer shall come to Zion speedily in our days, Amen, so may it be [His] will.
Pele Yoetz 344:1: Sheinah (Sleep) — We have learned a second time (Avot 3:10): sleep in the morning removes a person from the world. And it is a pity that this is forgotten, and especially in the summer months, when at the beginning of the night, while people are still up either checking their account books or in laughter and joyful company, and then sleep the sleep of the morning until the time for reciting the Shema and praying has passed, and when they rise from their sleep the world grows dark before them, for they wish to hurry to their shop for their business, and they say, after the time for the Shema has passed, “A hurried and truncated prayer” — “If your eyes fly to it, it is gone” — this is their foolish way, and they are not concerned to come to the synagogue except from Shabbat to Shabbat, or also on Mondays and Thursdays for half the prayer service.
Pele Yoetz 344:2: And Mahari, of blessed memory, already wrote in the book Kikar LaAden (p. 145), and these are his words: “Trembling has seized me, how the reins have been loosened to pray individually and even after the time for the Shema, for our sages, of blessed memory, said that one is liable to excommunication. And in the Midrash Konen they said that one is liable to excommunication for neglecting Kaddish and Kedushah. And our sages, of blessed memory, in the first chapter of Berachot (8a), and in the holy Zohar, elaborated greatly on the merit of praying with a congregation. And if it is bad to do this even once, the matter is an a fortiori argument regarding persisting in it, which is bad and bitter — may the Name bring us back in complete repentance and enlighten our eyes to be saved from the evil inclination,” thus far his words. And I have already said that now, through our sins, having lost every good thing, almost all our unity and all our Divine service to our Creator consists of these three prayers, and if even this is lacking, what are we and what is our life? And the Lord is righteous, for we have transgressed and rebelled, and this is why we have not been saved these several hundred years, and this is our undoing in this world or the World to Come, or both equally for evil, may the Merciful One save us. And the man who is a Jew and believes in the Torah and the words of our sages, of blessed memory, should have regard for his own soul and his Maker's honor, and not destroy himself knowingly, and while his eyes are still open, before the days of evil come when regret will be of no avail, upon hearing this and this and this, all that he did that was not good, let the man regret and abandon his evil way and walk in the way of the good, and he shall repent and be healed (and as I shall write further under the entry Shemi'ah).
Pele Yoetz 344:3: And they said in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 17:5) regarding the verse (Genesis 2:21), “And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall”: Rabbi Yehoshua, in the name of Rabbi Levi, said: the beginning of downfall is sleep, for since he is asleep he is not engaged in Torah nor in work — thus far. And especially for a Torah scholar, sleep harms him, for the song of Torah is only at night, and it is a time of favor to grieve over the destruction of the Holy Temple by reciting the order of Tikkun Chatzot, and to pour out speech and seek forgiveness, and a person can attain much greater perfection at night than by day, and in the holy Zohar and among the kabbalists they elaborated exceedingly greatly on the praise that comes to one who rises at midnight.
Pele Yoetz 344:4: And it is written in the books that it is better for a person to sleep several hours during the day so that he can rise at midnight, and although they said (Sukkah 26a) that it is forbidden to sleep during the day more than a horse's sleep, this was not said regarding one who wishes to rise early to study, or one who wishes to stay awake at night, for then it is a commandment to sleep during the day. And the wise man has already said: part of being careful is not to be overly careful. And just as it is good not to sleep during the day when there is no reason for it, so it is good to sleep in order to be awake at night, but one should not press himself to hold to both this and that, lest sleep overtake him during the Shema and prayer with tefillin, and his gain come out as his loss; and likewise in this manner, although they said it is good to stay awake all night on certain nights, such as the night of Shavuot and Hoshana Rabbah, and the kabbalists also wrote that it is very good to join night to day with words of Torah — in any case, if his eyes anticipate the watches and he sees that the bonds of sleep are falling upon him, and he fears he cannot withstand it during prayer, and therefore lies down to rest a little close to dawn so that he can stand and his mind be settled for prayer, it shall be counted as a commandment for him. And they already said (Nazir 23b): great is a transgression performed for its own sake. How much more so this, regarding which it is said (Psalms 112:5), “Good is the man who conducts his affairs with justice.”
Pele Yoetz 344:5: But a person should not incite sleep in himself, and even if the bonds of sleep fall upon him, let him press himself and rise and splash [water] on the floor and wash his face, until he accustoms himself to minimal sleep, for habit becomes second nature. And let him command all the members of his household with all firmness to stand guard to awaken him at the beginning of the watches, or at least to rise early for the morning prayer, and it goes without saying that if he awakens, he should not be lazy nor roll about in his bed until he falls back asleep, or until the congregational prayer passes, for it is explained in the holy Zohar that the Holy One, blessed be He, returns souls to Israel during the night to see who has understanding, and so that they have no excuse on the Day of Judgment for not having anticipated the watches, and the rooster crows lightly and they curse it with harsh curses for not having said, “Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night?” and they call it “rebuked by its master, abandoned by its master, rebuked” — meaning, from menstrual impurity, may the Merciful One save us.
Pele Yoetz 344:6: Over this let all who mourn mourn, and let the man tremble and shrink, and let a man gather strength and build fences for himself with restrictions, barriers, and penalties, to stand firm as a mighty man and gather strength to rise at the watches for the service of the blessed Creator, and how much more so if he lies down to sleep at the beginning of the night or during the day in order to rise at night, and sees that sleep flees from him — let him not roll about in bed for an hour or hours trying to grasp sleep with his hands, but rather rise and engage in Torah until sleep comes to him of itself. And whenever he can stay awake and engage in Torah, let him press himself to stay awake, and let him imagine himself as one who could earn a thousand thousand gold dinars, who has no desire to sleep for days and nights — how much more so for engaging in Torah and giving satisfaction to our Creator, for one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the World to Come (Avot 4:17). And days shall come in which there is no desire; “among the dead I am free” and he shall sleep much. And whatever a man desires, he can do — only its beginning is painful, and all beginnings are hard until one becomes accustomed, and according to the pain is the reward.
Pele Yoetz 344:7: And our master already wrote in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim, sec. 231) that even for the little he sleeps, his intention should not be for his body's pleasure, but rather to sustain his body for the service of the blessed Name — see there the whole section, words of the living God. And how good it is to say with a full mouth before sleeping: “Behold, I am lying down to sleep so that my mind be clear and settled for the service of the blessed Name.” And when lying down to sleep a little on the Shabbat day, let him say: “Behold, I am lying down to sleep for the delight of Shabbat,” as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yalkut Reuveni, Vaetchanan, an acronym of Shabbat): sleep on Shabbat is a delight, “And let the pleasantness [of the Lord be upon us],” etc. Whoever desires life should not incite sleep, which is one-sixtieth of death, for it is life we seek, in order to acquire through it the life of the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 345:1: Sichah (Conversation) — I have already written above under the entry Peh regarding the evil of the mouth, that one is not careful and does not guard against forbidden speech. And since the mouth runs swiftly and many have trampled upon this prohibition and treated it as permitted, I shall therefore repeat this chapter with the help of Heaven, and copy in brief the holy words of the pious master in the book Reshit Chokhmah, chapter 10 of the Gate of Holiness, with some additional elaboration, so that it be a reminder before our eyes — perhaps we can subdue the evil inclination so that it not rule over us, and the Lord God shall help us, Amen, so may it be [His] will.
Pele Yoetz 345:2: (1) Speech corresponds to the final Heh of the Name, and it is the “face of man” in the Divine Chariot.
Pele Yoetz 345:3: (2) It is written (Proverbs 11:13), “And a faithful spirit conceals a matter” — meaning, that he should be strong in his spirit not to let out a matter where it is not fitting.
Pele Yoetz 345:4: (3) That vanity which is for nothing — when the soul departs from him, it is rolled to it like a stone in a sling.
Pele Yoetz 345:5: (4) Vanity that is not holy ascends to the husk [kelipah] and builds vain structures, vanities that are deceptive fabrications, and there his soul shall ascend after his death.
Pele Yoetz 345:6: (5) It is fitting to sanctify one's mouth so that a matter of holiness not issue from a blemished vessel, in which the Holy One, blessed be He, does not dwell, since it is blemished, as it is written (Leviticus 21:18), “Any man who has a blemish shall not draw near.”
Pele Yoetz 345:7: (6) Whoever has a blemish in his mouth or his speech shall be liable to come into reincarnation to rectify what he distorted.
Pele Yoetz 345:8: (7) We have learned (Avot 1:17): I have found nothing better for the body than silence, and study is not the essential thing but rather action, and whoever increases words brings sin.
Pele Yoetz 345:9: (8) They said in the Talmud (Chullin 89b): Rabbi Yitzchak said, what is a person's craft in this world? Let him make himself like a mute. Explanation: just as through a craft one finds life, so through silence, for every vain word a person utters diminishes a portion of his life, and through silence he finds life.
Pele Yoetz 345:10: (9) It is written (Ecclesiastes 5:1), “Do not be hasty with your mouth, and let not your heart rush to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on the earth; therefore let your words be few.” This means: do not be hasty, so that no blemish be found in it, which is haste and a husk [kelipah]. “With your mouth” means that you should not blemish the Divine Presence, which is “upon your mouth.” “And let not your heart rush to utter a word before God” means: think that you are before Him and that He hears your words; if so, a matter of holiness that you speak before God — do not rush to utter it, but rather deliberate first. “For God is in heaven” means that He, with all His entourage, judges your every single utterance. “And you are on the earth” means that through silence you remove yourself from the earth, from the coarse matter within it, and become equal to the angels. Therefore let your words — even those that are for your own need and benefit — be few.
Pele Yoetz 345:11: (10) It is written (Amos 4:13), “For behold, He who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and tells man what is his speech.” Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Vayikra Rabbah 26:7) that even matters of no substance are written in a person's ledger and read before him at the time of his death — a pity for how many ledgers will fill up with this for one who is not careful.
